Title: Where work waits
Detail_lesson: Work spends far more time waiting than being worked on. The waiting almost always happens at a boundary between two people or two teams.
CustomInstruction: Identify the point where work sits idle longest on its way to done. Estimate the wait in hours or days, and name the handoff rather than the person.

Title: Context that never travels
Detail_lesson: Some context lives only in the head of whoever has been there longest, and gets re-explained every single time.
CustomInstruction: Name one thing you find yourself explaining repeatedly. Then propose exactly where it should live so the explaining stops.

Title: Done means what?
Detail_lesson: Teams agree that work should be finished and disagree quietly about what finished means. The disagreement surfaces at the worst moment.
CustomInstruction: State your team's real definition of done for one type of work - not the aspirational one. If two colleagues would answer differently, say so.

Title: Feedback you still use
Detail_lesson: Most advice evaporates. A small amount rewires how someone works for years, and it is worth knowing what makes the difference.
CustomInstruction: Recall advice that changed how you work and quote it as closely as you can. Then say what made it land: timing, the person, or the specificity.

Title: The unsaid note
Detail_lesson: Nearly everyone is carrying one piece of feedback they have decided not to give. The hard part is the opening sentence.
CustomInstruction: Think of feedback you are holding back, then write only the first sentence you would actually say out loud. No preamble, no softening paragraph.

Title: Praise that missed
Detail_lesson: Recognition that is too general reads as obligation. Recognition that names the specific act reads as attention.
CustomInstruction: Describe recognition that felt hollow, without naming who gave it. Then rewrite it so it points at one concrete thing that person did.

Title: Your best two hours
Detail_lesson: Deep work tends to happen in a narrow, predictable window that most calendars treat as ordinary time.
CustomInstruction: Say when your best thinking reliably happens and what currently protects it. Then name the single thing that most often takes that window away.

Title: The meeting you'd delete
Detail_lesson: Recurring meetings outlive their reason. The test is not whether the meeting is pleasant but whether anything breaks without it.
CustomInstruction: Pick one recurring meeting and describe what would concretely break if it disappeared next week. If nothing would break, say that plainly.

Title: Interrupt or queue?
Detail_lesson: Teams rarely agree on what deserves an interruption, so everything becomes urgent or nothing does.
CustomInstruction: Describe how a colleague should reach you for something genuinely time-critical. Then name one category of request that should never arrive that way.

Title: Where you go first
Detail_lesson: Written documentation and actual practice often diverge. What people really do when stuck is the more useful signal.
CustomInstruction: Name your actual first stop when you get stuck - a person, a document, a channel. Then say whether that would work for someone who joined next Monday.

Title: The bus-factor-one thing
Detail_lesson: Almost every team has a capability that rests on one person. It is usually known and rarely addressed.
CustomInstruction: Identify something only one person on your team can currently do. Then suggest the smallest realistic step that makes it two people.

Title: Documentation you trust
Detail_lesson: Trust in a document comes from a small number of signals: who owns it, when it last changed, and whether it contains a worked example.
CustomInstruction: Name a document you genuinely rely on and say which signal earns your trust. Then name one your team maintains that fails the same test.
